Author's own Go 1.24/1.25.1 benchmark (GODEBUG=fips140 on vs off): ECDSA P-256 keygen 17µs to 110µs (the per-key pairwise consistency test), crypto/rand 32 bytes 85ns to 355ns (DRBG construction); ECDSA signing and AES-256-GCM unchanged. Approved mode also bans ChaCha20-Poly1305 without AES hardware and Argon2.

Digital assets are structurally incompatible: secp256k1, Keccak-256, and RIPEMD-160 are not FIPS-approved (AWS CloudHSM offers secp256k1/Ed25519 only on non-FIPS clusters), and BIP32 keys off the 12-character 'Bitcoin seed' constant (96 bits, below the 112-bit HMAC floor), so fips140=only panics on the first derivation. The 90%-run-it-off figure is a single unverified vendor sales-engineer anecdote.
summary: A practitioner argues that FIPS 140-3 validation attests only that a specific module firmware and configuration implements approved algorithms correctly, and not that the surrounding product, key management, or operating configuration is secure. It marshals a history of certified-but-broken modules (ROCA, EUCLEAK, Dual_EC_DRBG, and a 2019 YubiKey bug caused by the FIPS self-test machinery itself) to show the certificate's scope excludes side channels, ceremonies, and configuration drift where real incidents occur. It documents the certification freeze: a 12-18 month CMVP queue forces vendors to keep shipping known-vulnerable validated builds, illustrated by Go's crypto module being certified two releases behind. Author-run Go benchmarks quantify FIPS mode's cost (roughly 6-9x on ECDSA keygen, 3-6x on random reads, none on signing or bulk AES) and note it buys no attack resistance. A detailed section shows cryptocurrency stacks (secp256k1, Keccak-256, RIPEMD-160, BIP32's sub-112-bit HMAC key) cannot run in approved mode, explaining why buyers reportedly disable it. The piece concludes that auditors accept the certificate in seconds and spend their time on key provenance, configuration attestation, quorum custody, and ceremony evidence; it recommends buying validated, attesting the actual running configuration on a schedule, and documenting in writing when FIPS mode is off.
novelty: FIPS certification history shows it certifies snapshots, not ongoing security
audience: security engineers, compliance/procurement leads dealing with crypto modules and HSMs

title: DiffusionGemma Technical Report
why: Converting an existing autoregressive model to discrete diffusion for under 10% of its original token budget yields roughly 1,500 output tokens/sec on one H100, a route to fast inference that skips training from scratch.
notes: DiffusionGemma is a fine-tune of the MoE Gemma 4 (3.8B activated, 25.2B total parameters), not a from-scratch model; it uses discrete diffusion to refine blocks of 256 tokens in parallel instead of decoding token by token.

Two-stage training: supervised fine-tuning teaches bidirectional denoising, then reinforcement learning combined with sampler distillation jointly targets generation quality and inference efficiency, using under 10% of the AR model's total training token budget.

Self-reported speed: averaged across the evaluation suite, ~20 tokens per forward pass and ~1,500 output tokens/sec on a single NVIDIA H100, claimed faster than AR models even with state-of-the-art speculative decoding.

Retains the base model's thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long-context support, and can still perform AR generation with only minor degradation, which the authors frame as a path to hybrid diffusion-AR decoding.
Labeled experimental open-weight; the abstract reports no benchmark accuracy numbers, hardware batch sizes, or the specific tasks in the 'full evaluation suite' behind the Pareto-frontier claim.
summary: DiffusionGemma is an experimental open-weight language model that applies discrete diffusion to text generation, iteratively refining 256-token blocks in parallel rather than decoding sequentially. It is produced by fine-tuning the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model (3.8B activated, 25.2B total parameters) with a two-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning for bidirectional denoising, followed by reinforcement learning plus sampler distillation, consuming under 10% of the original AR model's training token budget. The authors report roughly 20 tokens per forward pass and about 1,500 output tokens/sec on a single H100, which they claim beats AR models using state-of-the-art speculative decoding, and they position the result as a new speed-versus-capability Pareto frontier. The model retains thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts, and can still generate autoregressively with minor degradation, suggesting hybrid diffusion-AR decoding. The abstract provides no accuracy benchmarks or methodology detail, so quality and speed claims are self-reported.
novelty: diffusion fine-tune of Gemma hits 1,500 tok/s on one H100
audience: researchers/engineers working on LLM inference speed and diffusion LMs

title: Concurrency vs. Throughput: why more parallelism can make databases slower
why: If your workload has hot rows or long-lived transactions, raising a connection or transaction pool cap to make errors disappear can invert throughput: this postmortem shows a MySQL shard recover by cutting its pool from 10,000 to ~1,000.
notes: The 16-minute incident: a batch job held row locks for 15 minutes, forcing InnoDB to walk ever-longer MVCC version chains to build consistent snapshots for unrelated simple reads; reads that took milliseconds blew past a 90-second ceiling, apps retried in tight loops, and over 10,000 requests piled up until the buffer pool couldn't free memory. Errors peaked at 1,400/min as throughput fell from 15,000 to 1,500 qps.

The blocked reads were mostly not waiting on the locks themselves; the damage was snapshot reconstruction cost (coherency), which the article frames as the real failure mode versus focusing on 'lock contention.'

Migration from Cloud SQL (a queuing thread-pool that caps concurrent statements around 1,000 and makes clients wait) to Vitess vttablet's fail-fast transaction pool (waits a set time, then errors) exposed application code that had never handled pool-full errors.

The initial fix, raising the Vitess transaction pool to 10,000 (a number chosen to stop errors, not by sizing), removed backpressure and let InnoDB take on ~10,000 concurrent snapshot reads, worsening the coherency cost.

The framing uses Little's Law (N = X*W) and Gunther's Universal Scalability Law, X(N)=γN/(1+α(N−1)+βN(N−1)): the βN(N−1) coherency term quadruples when N doubles, and past N_max=√((1−α)/β) throughput reverses (retrograde scaling). Row locks map to α; snapshot rebuild cost maps to β.

Fix: cut the pool back to ~1,000 (the size the workload ran on for years) and queue with a longer bounded timeout instead of erroring. A later burst on a busier shard hit ~25,000 slot requests/s against ~1,000 slots with zero errors, flat ~60,000 qps, one rejected transaction all day, and fewer than 200 statements executing in MySQL at any instant (~3ms each by Little's Law). Vendor self-reported; scoped to contended/pessimistic-locking workloads, not universal.
summary: A PlanetScale postmortem details a 16-minute MySQL/Vitess outage triggered by a batch job that held row locks for 15 minutes. The open transaction forced InnoDB to rebuild ever-growing MVCC version chains for unrelated snapshot reads, so simple reads exceeded a 90-second timeout, applications retried, and over 10,000 requests accumulated until the buffer pool was overwhelmed. The workload had recently migrated from Cloud SQL's queuing thread-pool to Vitess's fail-fast transaction pool, exposing app code unprepared for pool-full errors; raising the pool cap to 10,000 removed backpressure and made contention worse. The authors explain the collapse with Little's Law and Gunther's Universal Scalability Law, arguing the coherency term (requests making each other slower, scaling with N(N-1)) drives retrograde scaling past N_max, and that this, not lock contention alone, caused the wider outage. The fix reverted the pool to about 1,000 slots and switched to bounded queuing instead of immediate errors; a later burst reaching ~25,000 slot requests/s against ~1,000 slots reportedly held ~60,000 qps flat with one rejected transaction all day. All performance figures are vendor self-reported, and the authors caution the advice applies to contended, pessimistic-locking workloads, not as a general rule.
novelty: postmortem quantifies InnoDB retrograde scaling via Gunther's USL
audience: backend/database engineers running MySQL/Vitess at scale

title: 99% of My Website Traffic Is Bots
why: If you run a content site, your JavaScript analytics are hiding a 200:1 bot-to-human ratio, and this post gives you the exact Cloudflare WAF rules to see it and cut it.
notes: The author's server served 1.28M full pages in a week while Plausible-style analytics recorded only 5,977 pageviews: roughly 214 bot page loads per human. On April 22 the 1.5M-page site took 3.6M requests from 361,844 unique IPs, nearly all in China; Cloudflare's Managed Challenge absorbed 1.18M in ten hours but many passed, prompting country-level blocks of China, then Vietnam and Singapore.

Self-measured pages-crawled-per-visitor-referred: Claude-SearchBot at 35,000:1 (420,680 pages requested in a week, 12 human visitors), versus Cloudflare's stated ~3,000:1 baseline. Bandwidth that week: 4.63 GB served to the bot, 175 KB to the humans it referred. Amazon's Amzn-SearchBot later became the top crawler at ~117,000 requests/day with zero referred visitors.

Blocking Claude-SearchBot at the firewall dropped it from ~60,000 requests/day to ~25/day: the author's evidence that declared crawlers honor a 403. Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control separately blocks declared training bots (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider) before custom rules run.

Challenge economics: over a 48-hour window Cloudflare issued 106,437 challenges with 252 solved, a 0.24% solve rate, the author's argument that challenges barely touch real users. Rule ordering matters: a 'skip for verified bots' rule sits after block rules so blocked bots stay blocked while Googlebot never sees a challenge.

Residential botnets defeat network defenses by design: thousands of rented home-ISP IPs, one request each, spoofing Chrome 118-120. Counter-rules challenge 46 datacenter ASNs and stale browser versions (Chrome 100-130), after checking only 0.54% of real search visitors run browsers that old (Firefox 115 ESR exempted).

Costs and caveat: whole site runs ~$90/month on Cloudflare Workers, D1, and KV, spiking ~500% in one bad month; edge caching makes bots a nuisance rather than an existential VPS bill. The author frames the only durable fix as economic (Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl), and notes he is himself a scraper, building the database from IRS 990 forms and public donor walls.
summary: The operator of PatronView, a 1.5M-page database of American philanthropists, documents a year of fighting scrapers and finds that bots account for roughly 99% of traffic: 1.28M full pages served in a week versus 5,977 pageviews recorded by JavaScript analytics. He introduces a working metric, pages crawled per visitor referred, and measures Claude-SearchBot at 35,000:1 against Cloudflare's stated ~3,000:1 baseline, with Amazon's Amzn-SearchBot later topping crawlers at ~117,000 requests/day and no referred visitors. Blocking these AI crawlers at the firewall cut Claude from ~60,000 to ~25 requests/day, evidence that declared bots respect a 403, though the training bots are also caught earlier by Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control. Country blocks (China, Vietnam, Singapore) handled a 3.6M-request-per-day flood, datacenter-ASN and stale-browser challenges caught cloud and residential botnets, and a 0.24% CAPTCHA solve rate over 106,437 challenges is offered as proof the defenses spare humans. The post lists every Cloudflare WAF rule expression verbatim, notes residential proxy networks remain unstoppable at the network layer, and argues the real fix is economic via pay-per-crawl. All crawler ratios and traffic figures are the author's own self-reported measurements from a single site.
novelty: measured pages-crawled-per-visitor ratios for AI bots vs stated benchmarks
audience: engineers/founders running high-traffic sites dealing with scraper/bot load and infra costs

title: Managing AI Coding Costs at Scale
why: If your org's agentic-coding bill is on an exponential curve, the cheapest lever isn't a spend cap: it's tracking the "efficiency frontier" and staying free to swap models, which Databricks says cut its generated tokens and cost roughly in half with no quality drop.
notes: The core distinction: chase the efficiency frontier (best price per fixed intelligence level) rather than the intelligence frontier; the authors claim efficiency-frontier models ship almost weekly and advance faster than peak intelligence, since most coding does not need frontier-level reasoning.

Model independence is the enabling mechanism. Databricks open-sourced/made free two components: Omnigent, a meta-harness that presents one UX while dispatching to underlying harnesses (proprietary and open source), and Unity AI Gateway for central model-menu management, cost observability, and context/cache control. Alternative is asking devs to switch between Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, which risks harness lock-in to a model family.

Self-reported eval results (all vendor/company claims, model names as stated): Stripe found Opus 4.7 gave no meaningful quality gain over 4.6 at higher cost and declined to deploy it; Databricks saw a cost regression comparing Opus 5.0 to 4.8, and found GLM models price/performance-competitive, leading to internal rollout.

Hard token budgets are called a last-resort control, not the primary lever: cutting off a developer at a ceiling hurts productivity, and top spenders are often the highest-output users. Preferred approach is near-real-time spend visibility across tools plus progressive friction as spend rises.

Cost is dominated by context the user never typed: tool calls, codebase search, injected skills/system info. Databricks says tuning harness and prompt-caching settings (cache writes cost money, cached reads cut per-inference cost) yielded an almost 50% reduction in generated tokens and cost with no observed quality degradation.

Evidence base is an informal, self-described 'directional' survey of Databricks plus Stripe, Coinbase, Uber, and Ramp; the savings table and benchmarks are internal and not accompanied by public methodology. Thrive Capital gave feedback on an early draft.
summary: A Databricks engineering post lays out a playbook for keeping agentic-coding costs inside a roughly fixed per-user envelope while preserving broad, low-friction access. Its central argument is to optimize for the "efficiency frontier" (cheapest model meeting the quality bar for typical engineering work) rather than the intelligence frontier, since efficiency-frontier models ship faster and most coding does not need frontier reasoning. Capturing those gains requires model independence, which Databricks addresses with two open-sourced/free tools: Omnigent, a meta-harness that dispatches to underlying harnesses, and Unity AI Gateway for central model management, cost observability, and context/cache control. The post reports company-specific eval results as claims (Stripe declining Opus 4.7 over 4.6; Databricks seeing an Opus 5.0-vs-4.8 regression and rolling out GLM), and argues against hard budgets in favor of spend visibility plus progressive friction. It also stresses that most cost comes from injected context, not user prompts, and says caching and harness tuning cut Databricks' generated tokens and cost by nearly 50% with no observed quality loss. The evidence is a self-described informal, directional survey of Databricks, Stripe, Coinbase, Uber, and Ramp, without published benchmark methodology.
novelty: the "efficiency frontier" outpaces intelligence frontier for coding cost control
audience: engineering leaders managing AI coding tool spend at scale

title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
why: If you let Gemini CLI or Qwen Code load third-party skill folders, this paper measures how often a hidden shell command inside a natural-language skill file actually runs: 95.5-96.1% and 71.6-74.0% of the time, with the agent noticing the malice in under 2% of runs.
notes: Attack surface is the agent skills interface: folders of instructions and scripts loaded dynamically, where malicious shell commands can hide inside benign-looking natural-language files.
Benchmark: 2,826 adversarial skills synthesized from 471 real-world shell commands using six LLMs across four families, mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics; code and dataset released.
Exploit rates over 5,629 completed runs: Gemini CLI 95.5-96.1%, Qwen Code 71.6-74.0% (raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected range), nearly invariant to which model generated the skill.
Explicit safety recognition, meaning the agent flags malicious intent, happened in only 1.99% of runs.

Evaluation pipeline uses run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override with a three-judge LLM panel, validated against a blind human gold standard at Cohen's kappa = 0.85.
Self-reported by the authors and limited to two agents; results are exploit-rate measurements, not evidence of in-the-wild attacks.
summary: The paper quantifies how easily coding agents execute malicious shell commands hidden inside their skill files, the folders of instructions and scripts agents load to specialize behavior. The authors synthesize 2,826 benign-appearing adversarial skills from 471 real shell commands using six LLMs across four families, mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and release the benchmark. Across 5,629 completed runs, they report Gemini CLI is exploited in 95.5-96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6-74.0%, with rates nearly independent of which model generated the skill and explicit safety recognition occurring in just 1.99% of runs. Judgments come from a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel with run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's kappa = 0.85). The authors argue enterprises must assess and mitigate skill-interface risk before adopting coding agents. Results are self-reported and confined to two agents, so they measure exploitability rather than observed real-world attacks.
novelty: first quantified exploit rate for coding-agent "skill files" attack surface
audience: security engineers and teams deploying autonomous coding agents like Gemini CLI/Qwen Code

title: To Add Is Machine, To Delete Is Human: Measuring and Mitigating Deletion Avoidance in LLM Code Editing
why: If you let an LLM close bugs against a passing test suite, roughly one in three of its patches wraps dead code in a guard instead of removing it, so your codebase accretes cruft that your tests never catch.
notes: Across the top five SWE-bench Verified models, deletion recall against the developer patch tops out at 71.7% even on tasks all five solve; models reach the correct file for over 92% of required deletions but cut the exact line in under 52% of cases.
29.0% of passing patches use what the authors call Guard-and-Go: wrapping code that should be deleted in a guard or fallback. These pass because the original tests rarely check for removal.
Retrofitting 34 Verified tasks with tests that fail if the targeted code remains dropped four frontier models (closed and open weights) from 63.2% to 41.9% success.
CanItDelete, a new benchmark of 200 tasks from real commits where the entire required edit is deletion, still defeats the best model on one task in five; smaller open models fall to 18.0%.

Ablating GPT-5.6 Sol under four cumulative prompts moved success little until exact lines were supplied; even then success only reached 80.5% because the model over-deletes past the spans or adds code instead.

A pilot fix: teaching deletion during post-training reduced deletion avoidance and improved broader code-editing, which the authors read as the behavior being undertrained rather than out of reach. Numbers are self-reported by the authors.
summary: The paper identifies and quantifies "deletion avoidance," the systematic tendency of LLM code editors to retain code that an intended edit requires removing. On SWE-bench Verified, the top five models reach at most 71.7% deletion recall against developer patches even on commonly solved tasks, and though they find the right file over 92% of the time, they cut the exact required line under 52% of the time; 29.0% of passing patches instead wrap the code in a guard or fallback, a pattern the authors name Guard-and-Go, which survives because original tests rarely check for removal. When 34 Verified tasks are retrofitted with tests that fail if targeted code remains, four frontier models drop from 63.2% to 41.9%. The authors release CanItDelete, 200 pure-deletion tasks from real commits, where the best model still fails one task in five and smaller open models fall to 18.0%; supplying GPT-5.6 the exact lines to delete only lifts success to 80.5% because it then over-deletes or adds code. A post-training pilot reduced the behavior and improved general code editing, suggesting it is undertrained. All figures are the authors' self-reported results.
novelty: names and quantifies "deletion avoidance" / Guard-and-Go failure mode in LLM code edits
audience: engineers using/evaluating LLM coding agents and researchers building code-editing benchmarks

title: Introducing Kitesurf: The agent-first browser that runs in V8 isolates on Cloudflare Workers
why: If you run agents that drive headless browsers through Cloudflare's Browser Run, there is now a Chromium alternative that Cloudflare's own benchmarks put at 3-7x less memory and CPU per session, at the cost of being ~1.7x slower on wall time.
notes: Architecture: a browser with no Chromium, running across V8 isolates on Workers. Three main components. The Engine holds session state and speaks Chrome DevTools Protocol (so Puppeteer, Playwright, chrome-remote-interface, and MCP-over-CDP clients work by adding browser=kitesurf); PageScript spins up a Dynamic Worker isolate per page/OOPIF to parse HTML/CSS and run JS; PageRenderer rasterizes to PNG/JPEG/PDF and is called stateless over Workers RPC so it can be killed and retried.

Built from Rust compiled to Wasm via wasm-bindgen (avoiding Emscripten emulation), reusing Blitz (rendering), Stylo (Firefox CSS parser), Parley (text shaping), and blitz-paint. eval is unsupported natively in Workers, so it runs Boa JS, a Rust ECMAScript engine, as a runtime-on-a-runtime until native eval lands.

Cloudflare's self-reported medians over five runs on a 14-URL corpus: screenshot CPU 380ms vs Chromium 1,173ms (3.1x), HTML-extraction CPU 229ms vs 877ms (3.8x); screenshot memory 57.8 MiB vs 271 MiB (4.7x), extraction memory 39.4 vs 273.7 MiB (7.0x). Chromium wins wall time: screenshot 1,148ms vs 637ms, extraction 820ms vs 472ms (~1.7x slower), attributed to cold software rasterization and image encoding versus a warm JIT.

Passes 215,000+ Web Platform Tests (conformance to W3C standards, not real-site fidelity); coverage claimed good for CSS, DOM, HTML, selection, SVG, XHR. Validated additionally with Puppeteer visual-regression runs against Chromium.

Explicit limits: no video playback, no WebGL, no bot-challenge TLS-fingerprint handshakes, no long authenticated persistent-state sessions; Cloudflare says use the Chromium default for those. Every page load treated as untrusted, sessions start fresh, failures degrade to blank frames rather than crashing; SandboxOutbound is the sole network egress, enforcing CORS, cookie jars, and 403 on policy failures.

12 weeks old (first commit May), free in beta behind per-account limits via Browser Run, with a public playground that injects DevTools and reports per-isolate Wasm memory. Cloudflare says it plans to open-source Kitesurf so customers can self-deploy.
summary: Cloudflare announced Kitesurf, a headless browser built specifically for AI agents that runs entirely in V8 isolates on Cloudflare Workers instead of using Chromium. It is written largely in Rust compiled to WebAssembly via wasm-bindgen, reusing Firefox's Stylo CSS parser and the Blitz/Parley rendering stack, and uses Boa JS to handle eval because Workers lack native eval support. The design splits work across a stateful Engine that speaks Chrome DevTools Protocol and stateless PageScript and PageRenderer isolates connected by Workers RPC, so failed renders can be killed and retried, with all network egress funneled through a single SandboxOutbound worker. Cloudflare's own benchmarks over a 14-URL corpus report 3-7x lower CPU and memory than a warm Chromium pool but roughly 1.7x slower wall time, and the browser passes 215,000+ Web Platform Tests. It does not yet support video, WebGL, real TLS-fingerprint bot challenges, or long authenticated sessions, for which Cloudflare recommends its Chromium default. Kitesurf is free in beta via Browser Run behind per-account limits, accessible by adding browser=kitesurf, with a public playground and a stated plan to open-source it for customer self-hosting.
novelty: agent-only browser built on Wasm/Rust in Cloudflare Workers, not Chromium
audience: devs building AI agents that need scalable, cheap browser automation

title: AI-generated vulnerability patches require human review
why: If your team is wiring LLM agents into vulnerability remediation, this study says the default outcome on hard patches is wrong more than half the time, so a domain-expert reviewer is not optional.
notes: 1Password's new Off-by-1 Labs generated 6,080 patches (400 flagged and removed) across six recently disclosed CVEs using two cyber-capable reasoning models: ChatGPT-5.5 (Trusted Access for Cyber, medium effort) and Anthropic Opus 4.8 (Cyber Verification Program, high effort). 540 patches per vulnerability per model, in sets of 20 across three environment configs and nine per-vulnerability prompt templates.

Self-reported outcomes: 26.0% fully fixed without altering app behavior (S1), 20.1% fixed but changed behavior (S2, e.g. reimplementing parsers, flipping allow-list to deny-list), and 53.9% FLAWED (Fix-Like Artifacts with Embedded Defects) that failed to fix, added a new vuln, or both (S3/S4/S5).

CVEs were chosen for recency to sit past model training cutoffs and avoid contamination: CVE-2026-31431 (Linux privesc), CVE-2026-34197 (ActiveMQ RCE), CVE-2026-8512 (Chrome File System Access UAF on macOS), CVE-2026-45185 (EXIM RCE), CVE-2026-22738 (SpringAI SpEL RCE), and GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g (Gemini CLI RCE). The authors hypothesized >67% success and got well below that.

Over 33% of the passing S1/S2 patches were judged 'fragile': narrow input guards rather than root-cause fixes. For the SpringAI CVE both models often just escaped the specific PoC characters, leaving the vulnerable code exploitable via alternative inputs.
Inference cost averaged $2.11 per patch/validation cycle for ChatGPT-5.5 and $2.81 for Opus 4.8; the paper flagged and excluded runs where a model appeared to retrieve the real upstream patch.

Anthropic (which reviewed the research) recommends execution-grounded verification over inspection-based checks with domain experts as final reviewers; 1Password released the full dataset, tooling, and paper 'Frontier Models' Vulnerability Patches are Often F.L.A.W.E.D.' All numbers are the authors' self-reported results, and per-model, per-CVE breakdowns live in the paper, not the blog post.
summary: 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs generated 6,080 candidate patches (400 flagged and dropped) for six recently disclosed, complex open-source CVEs using two cyber-tuned frontier reasoning models, ChatGPT-5.5 and Anthropic Opus 4.8. They report that only 26.0% of patches fully resolved the vulnerability without changing application behavior, 20.1% fixed it but altered behavior, and 53.9% were 'FLAWED': they failed to fix the bug, introduced a new one, or both. The CVEs were selected for recency to sit past training cutoffs and reduce data contamination, spanning Linux, ActiveMQ, Chrome, EXIM, SpringAI, and Gemini CLI. Even among passing patches, more than a third were 'fragile,' guarding the specific proof-of-concept input rather than the root cause. Per-patch inference cost averaged $2.11 (ChatGPT-5.5) and $2.81 (Opus 4.8). The team released the dataset, tooling, and a paper, and concludes that current models patch only a narrow subset of the vulnerabilities they can find, so human domain experts remain necessary as final reviewers.
novelty: first rigorous study using post-training-cutoff CVEs to test LLM patch quality
audience: security engineers and AI safety researchers evaluating automated patching tools

title: Security is Hard, Y’all
why: A legitimate Cloudflare launch tripped every consent-phishing alarm a trained security engineer has, and even Cloudflare's own AI chat agent labeled the real site a phishing attack, showing why URL-reputation defenses false-positive at scale.
notes: Cloudflare's new 'Wallet' feature was hosted on cloudflare.pay rather than cloudflare.com/pay or pay.cloudflare.com; there is no technical trust link between a company's .com and a separately registered .pay domain.
.pay is an open sTLD: any domain costs about $20 with no vetting, so an attacker could register cloudflarepayments.pay in minutes, unlike the vetted .bank sTLD.

A green checkmark intended as a hover-to-reveal security detail read as a spoofable trust badge, echoing how OAuth phishers put fake checkmarks and icons in app display names to trick Microsoft account consent screens.

When asked, Cloudflare's own AI support chat agent confirmed the legitimate site was a phishing attack; the agent also first requested full account control before the author downgraded it to read-only.
Reporting was broken: the permission page had no in-context 'report suspicious request' link, and the HackerOne channel was unreachable because a Cloudflare CAPTCHA on the login failed.

Author Eric Lawrence, a longtime browser/security engineer, prescribes hosting new features under the existing trusted domain, showing security info in a trustworthy place, and making scam reporting trivial and monitored; he closes by telling security folks never to blame victims.
summary: Eric Lawrence walks through trying to claim a handle on Cloudflare's new 'Wallet' product and finding that the legitimate flow was indistinguishable from a consent-phishing attack. The signals: the entry point lived on cloudflare.pay instead of cloudflare.com, the .pay sTLD is buyable for about $20 with no vetting, a security 'checkmark' looked like a spoofable trust badge, and the OAuth-style permission page offered no way to report a suspicious request. When he asked Cloudflare's AI support agent, it wrongly confirmed the real site was phishing, and the HackerOne reporting path was blocked by a broken CAPTCHA. His prescription for developers: keep new features under the trusted domain (or link to them directly from it), surface security information where users make decisions, and make in-context scam reporting easy and monitored. The broader point is that when legitimate sites behave this phishily, reputation services like SmartScreen and SafeBrowsing face an impossible false-positive problem, and phishing victims should not be blamed.
novelty: real Cloudflare product looked indistinguishable from consent phishing
audience: security engineers and UX/product teams designing OAuth consent and permission flows

title: Don’t stop early: Case-folding source code at memory speed
why: If you write hot-loop text code, this shows a measured 15x jump on ASCII case-folding (3.1 to >45 GiB/s) that comes from deleting an early-exit branch so the compiler can vectorize, plus a 1776-byte Unicode table that folds in byte space without ever decoding a code point.
notes: Scale motivation: GitHub's Blackbird code search indexes 180M+ repos and 480TB, case-folding every byte before ngram extraction and again per candidate match. Released as the Rust crate 'casefold'.

ASCII ladder on Apple M4 (5.7 KB buffer): naive branchy loop with early-exit break 3.1 GiB/s, 0 vector instrs; branchless body but keeping the break 2.6 GiB/s (slower, extra store traffic); dropping the break 7.6 GiB/s (partial vectorization); fully branchless test+write >45 GiB/s (full NEON, ~memory bandwidth). The data-dependent loop exit alone is what blocks vectorization; branchless is a pessimization in scalar code and only pays off as a vectorization enabler.

Folding is not lowercasing: folding is context-free and locale-independent (uses CaseFolding.txt statuses C and S), so if A matches B it does so symmetrically in any locale. The crate implements only simple 1-to-1 folds, skipping full folds (ss) and Turkic locale folds, matching ripgrep's choice for cross-tool consistency.

Unicode table is 1776 bytes (~9.6 bits/fold entry) covering Unicode 16.0's 1484 simple folds, versus ~11.6 KB naive, ~70 KB regex-syntax, ~7.3 KB Go, ~17 KB runtime HashMap. Layout: 64-code-point pages (folds touch 59 of ~1960), a 1-bit-per-page bitmap for a decode-free negative test straight from lead UTF-8 bytes, 238 packed runs (start/end/stride/delta, borrowed from Go's CaseRange), and an 8-wide SWAR compare over run keys.

The claimed-new part: fold as little-endian byte addition. Reading a character's UTF-8 bytes as a u32 and adding a per-run BYTE_DELTA yields the folded encoding directly, advancing by folded length, so length-changing folds (Kelvin U+212A to k; U+023A to a 3-byte char) work without decode/encode. Article claims ICU, Go, Rust regex, CPython, and glibc all decode first. Caveat: assumes well-formed shortest-form UTF-8; raw non-str bytes must be validated first.

Throughput vs real folders producing identical output (illustrative, auto-vectorization/SWAR/little-endian dependent): pure ASCII >45 GiB/s vs simd_normalizer 1.21 GiB/s and naive HashMap 213 MiB/s; CJK no-fold 2.95 GiB/s; worst-case all-folding Latin/Greek/Cyrillic 869 MiB/s (roughly tied with simd_normalizer's 922 MiB/s, about 2x slower than a simdutf decode/encode round-trip upper bound). Also >50% faster than the non-equivalent str::to_lowercase.
summary: GitHub engineering describes optimizing Unicode case folding for its Blackbird code search, which folds every byte across 180M+ repos and 480TB before building ngram indexes. The central finding is counterintuitive: the fastest ASCII path removes an optimization rather than adding one. A naive loop that breaks early on the first non-ASCII byte runs at 3.1 GiB/s with no vectorization; a data-dependent early exit is enough to keep the loop scalar. Deleting the break (OR-accumulating high bits to detect non-ASCII after the loop, using arithmetic masks instead of conditional stores) lets LLVM emit NEON and hit >45 GiB/s, near memory bandwidth, a ~15x gain. The Unicode fallback path compresses 1484 simple folds into a 1776-byte structure (page bitmap plus 238 packed runs with SWAR search) and, in the piece the authors call genuinely new, performs each fold as a little-endian u32 byte-space addition that skips UTF-8 decode and re-encode, handling length-changing folds by advancing the write cursor. All figures are self-reported on an Apple M4 and explicitly described as microarchitecture-dependent; the crate is open-sourced as 'casefold' and implements only simple 1-to-1 folds.
novelty: removing early-exit branch enables SIMD, 15x speedup
audience: systems/performance engineers working on text processing or search infra

title: Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids
why: The white-label reality: a $30 kids' watch and dozens of differently-branded ones share the same unauthenticated Chinese backend, so a single flaw exposes tens of millions of GPS trackers to silent tracking, eavesdropping, and camera capture.
notes: Stykas and Solferini analyzed 70+ GPS watches and car accessories for Black Hat and traced them to three Shenzhen supply chains: YiQingTeng/Wonlex/SETracker (30+ brands), NewGPS2012 (30+ brands), and SinoTrack, together covering tens of millions of devices.

Demonstrated live on a WIRED reporter wearing a $30 CJC/YiQingTeng watch: location tracking via nearby Wi-Fi identifiers even with GPS broken, silent photo capture, and live microphone audio, with no on-device indication. The reporter supplied only his registered email; SETracker's auth flaw let anyone send commands to any device.

SinoTrack: a demo account could command any device, plus a SQL injection exposing tens of thousands of devices' locations, passwords, and vehicle records. NewGPS2012: SQL injection, remote code execution, and evidence of a prior compromise by unknown parties.

Vendors were warned for months. SETracker emailed WIRED that issues were 'resolved long before,' then patched only hours before the talk after WIRED provided exploit evidence; SinoTrack and NewGPS2012 did not respond and their techniques still work.

Full vulnerability details withheld because not all are fixed; WIRED could not independently confirm each branded device, and car-unlock/disable message spoofing was found but not tested on real vehicles.
Prior warnings span years: Stykas/Gruhn's 2018 Trackmageddon, Pen Test Partners and Norway (2017-2018), and a 2020 Münster study that found serious flaws in five of six kids' watches.
summary: At Black Hat, researchers Vangelis Stykas and Felipe Solferini report that 70+ GPS-enabled children's smartwatches and car trackers reduce to just three Shenzhen backends: YiQingTeng/Wonlex/SETracker, NewGPS2012, and SinoTrack, collectively behind tens of millions of devices. All three had serious flaws, including missing authentication that let anyone command any device, SQL injection exposing device locations and passwords, and server-side remote code execution; NewGPS2012 also showed signs of a prior compromise. On a $30 CJC/YiQingTeng watch, they demonstrated live tracking (via Wi-Fi identifiers even with GPS broken), silent photo capture, and microphone eavesdropping on a WIRED reporter who had supplied only his registered email. The core point is that the white-label model makes consumer 'choice' among brands illusory, since a flaw in one backend affects dozens of brands at once. Despite months of warnings, SETracker claimed the issues were already fixed and patched only hours before the talk, while SinoTrack and NewGPS2012 did not respond and remain exploitable. The findings echo years of prior warnings (Trackmageddon 2018, Pen Test Partners, Norway, and a 2020 Münster study) that went largely unheeded.
novelty: supply-chain analysis reveals 3 Shenzhen platforms power 70+ vulnerable GPS trackers
audience: security researchers, IoT/embedded engineers, privacy-conscious parents

title: What AI Red-Team Evaluations Can and Cannot Prove
why: If you cite a passing safety benchmark as evidence a model won't cause rare catastrophic harm, this paper shows the math says your evaluation is orders of magnitude too small to support that claim.
notes: Defines an 'evidential ceiling': the largest factor by which one evaluation result can move belief under a fixed testing budget, derived in closed form for the benchmark null (clean-sheet) result.

Claims a computable crossover harm rate: above it, a modest-sized benchmark certifies a harm category to a stated evidentiary standard and a clean sheet outweighs a single reproduced failure; below it, no feasibly sized passive benchmark provides the specified evidence of safety under a fixed scoring rule and approximately independent trials.

Reframes evidential worth as discrimination between hypotheses rather than attack success, so the bound (written via hypothesis-conditioned elicitation rates) also covers adaptive and automated red teaming, not just static benchmarks.
Audits eight evaluation suites against the boundary: adequate for high-frequency harm categories, several orders of magnitude short for rare, catastrophic ones.

The argument is theoretical/statistical; the abstract states results in closed form but the provided text gives no empirical validation beyond the eight-suite audit, and the specific harm-rate threshold values and named suites are not listed here.
summary: This arXiv paper argues that the boundary between claims a red-team evaluation can and cannot support is calculable rather than a matter of judgment. It defines the 'evidential ceiling' as the largest factor by which one result can shift belief under a fixed testing budget, derives it in closed form for the benchmark null result, and identifies a closed-form crossover harm rate. Above that rate, a modest benchmark certifies a harm category to a stated evidentiary standard and a clean sheet outweighs one reproduced failure; below it, no feasibly sized passive benchmark provides the stated evidence of safety under a fixed scoring rule and approximately independent trials. Written in terms of hypothesis-conditioned elicitation rates, the bound generalizes to adaptive and automated red teaming, and shows that discrimination between hypotheses, not attack success, determines evidential worth. Auditing eight evaluation suites, the authors report they are adequate for high-frequency harms but several orders of magnitude short for rare, catastrophic ones. The conclusion is that safety benchmarks are informative about a specific, computable set of propositions and should state which.
novelty: closed-form limit on what red-team benchmarks can statistically prove
audience: AI safety researchers and evaluators designing red-team benchmarks

title: Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System (2025)
why: If you run or debug LLM serving, this maps vLLM's actual code paths, the scheduler, KV-cache manager, and allocate_slots, so you can reason about throughput and latency instead of treating the engine as a black box.
notes: Engine core anatomy: a Processor tokenizes inputs into EngineCoreRequests, the Scheduler (FCFS or priority) picks requests per step, and the KV-cache manager owns a free_block_queue of KV blocks (often hundreds of thousands) with 16 tokens per block by default; allocate_slots computes ceil(new_tokens/16) blocks and can trigger recompute preemption when the pool is exhausted.

The V1 scheduler mixes prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bandwidth-bound) requests in the same step, unlike V0 which handled only one type at a time; sequences are flattened into one concatenated super-sequence with position indices and masks so continuous batching needs no right-padding.

Worker init runs device setup, model load (optional torch.compile), and KV-cache init: a profiling forward pass takes a memory snapshot to size KV blocks under gpu_memory_utilization (e.g. 0.8), then CUDA graphs are captured per warmup batch size unless --enforce-eager, replaying a pre-baked DAG to cut kernel-launch overhead.

Prefix caching (on by default) hashes 16-token chunks (built-in hash or slower SHA-256) into BlockHash entries in cached_block_hash_to_block; find_longest_cache_hit does a linear search to reuse KV blocks, speeding prefill only, not decode.

Guided decoding compiles a grammar to an FSM (via third-party backends like xgrammar) and masks disallowed logits to -inf; the _grammar_bitmask packs allowed tokens as bits and expands 32x to vocab size using 32-bit words. Speculative decoding (n-gram, EAGLE, Medusa; no draft-LLM method in V1) proposes k tokens verified by one large-model pass, with a rejection sampler that keeps output statistically equal to autoregressive sampling.

Scaling path runs from InprocClient/UniProcExecutor (single GPU, offline, synchronous) to DPLBAsyncMPClient/MultiProcExecutor across GPUs and nodes with DP/TP/PP/EP; disaggregated P/D splits N prefill and M decode instances communicating KV through a connector (SharedStorageConnector shown as a debug example) to control TTFT and ITL. Hybrid models (Jamba's Transformer/SSM mix) need a more complex KV allocator per the Jenga reference.
summary: This is the first post in a series dissecting how vLLM implements high-throughput LLM inference, following an inverse-pyramid from a high-level mental model down to subsystems. It walks the offline single-GPU path first: the LLM engine constructor (config, processor, engine core client, output processor), the engine core's model executor, scheduler, and paged-attention KV-cache manager, and the step() loop of schedule, forward pass, and postprocess. It explains scheduling of compute-bound prefill versus memory-bandwidth-bound decode, block allocation via allocate_slots with 16-token blocks and preemption, and how flattening sequences enables continuous batching. It then covers advanced features: chunked prefill, prefix caching via block hashing and reuse, grammar-FSM guided decoding with bitmask logit masking, speculative decoding (n-gram, EAGLE, Medusa) with a rejection sampler, and disaggregated prefill/decode. Later posts are promised on scaling to multi-GPU/multi-node execution, the serving layer, and benchmarking/auto-tuning. All specifics are drawn from the author's reading of vLLM's V1 code, with third-party backends (e.g. xgrammar) noted as external.
novelty: deep technical walkthrough of vLLM internals, first in a series
audience: ML systems/infra engineers building or tuning LLM inference serving stacks

title: Towards Physics of Multimodal Pretraining: Knowledge Flow, Modality Synergy, Early Unification, and Recipes
why: If you are training unified vision-language models, the paper claims you can hit strong generative quality at 5% of the usual compute by unifying modalities early and using shared attention with modality-specific feed-forward layers.
notes: 'Vision laziness': the authors report that delaying modality integration pushes models to lean on language priors instead of learning from visual signal; early joint training is claimed to outperform late alignment or sequential training.

The recommended architecture shares attention and normalization across modalities but keeps feed-forward layers modality-specific; the authors say this promotes synergy over competition and holds across different visual tokenizer designs.
Data 'complexity' is presented as the main knob determining whether modalities help or fight each other during joint training.
Claimed 'recipes' reach strong generative performance using only 5% of the compute budget; the baseline being compared against is not specified in the abstract.
Findings are said to be validated at scale by training multiple 13.5B-parameter MoE models on 2T tokens; per-task benchmark numbers and methodology are not in the abstract.

Study covers three modalities, language, visual understanding, and visual generation, and reports asymmetric knowledge transfer among them; specifics are self-reported and not detailed in the abstract.
summary: This arXiv paper presents a systematic empirical study of how modalities interact during natively unified multimodal pretraining, using controlled experiments on synthetic and real-world data. It offers four claims: knowledge transfers asymmetrically among language, visual understanding, and visual generation; data complexity determines whether modalities are synergistic or competitive, with shared attention and normalization plus modality-specific feed-forward layers promoting synergy across tokenizer designs; unifying modalities from early training beats late alignment or sequential training and avoids a 'vision laziness' failure where models fall back on language priors; and derived recipes reach strong generative performance at 5% of the compute budget. The authors say they validated these findings by training multiple 13.5B MoE models on 2T tokens. The abstract does not report specific benchmark scores, baselines, or the methodology behind the 5% compute figure, so the quantitative claims remain self-reported.
novelty: systematic study of how modalities interact in unified pretraining
audience: researchers/engineers building multimodal foundation models

title: rust-lang/rust is adopting an LLM policy
why: If you contribute to rust-lang/rust, LLM-generated PRs now must carry tests and disclosure, must avoid soundness-critical code, and can be closed no-questions-asked when they touch docs, diagnostics, or unsafe internals.
notes: Scope: adopted by five teams for the rust-lang/rust monorepo only, explicitly not a project-wide or official Rust stance; the author says Rust operates by consensus and has no BDFL to ban or bless LLMs outright.

Organizing rule: 'It's fine to use LLMs to answer questions, analyze, distill, refine, check, suggest, review. But not to create.' Creation uses are heavily restricted; assistive uses are allowed, sometimes with disclosure.

Code changes held to a higher bar than human PRs: LLM PRs must have tests 'full stop,' must be pre-arranged, non-critical, high-quality, well-reviewed; LLMs must not generate soundness-critical changes unless the author is already a domain expert, and even then it's discouraged.

Disclosure is the bright-line rule: required for all public LLM text (translation, trivial changes, bug discovery, LLM-assisted review) unless exempted; private LLM output you don't ask others to read needs no disclosure. Reviewers aren't obligated to read LLM PRs.

Stated motivation is reviewer bandwidth and trust: 1,281 open PRs at time of writing; polished output no longer signals effort or understanding; autonomous agents mean 'no one on the other end'; copy-pasting review comments into an LLM and back is called a breach of trust.

Enforcement: reviewers may close non-compliant PRs and point authors to #llm-mentoring; authors, not reviewers, are responsible for declaring LLM use (a PR template will ask); 'style is not evidence,' and harassment of LLM users is barred under the Code of Conduct.
summary: Five teams in the Rust project adopted a policy, authored by one contributor, governing how large language models may be used when contributing to the rust-lang/rust monorepo; it is deliberately scoped to that repo and is not an official project-wide position. The policy replaces prior ad hoc 'wild west' moderation with published rules built around one line: LLMs are fine for answering, analyzing, refining, checking, and reviewing, but not for creating. LLM-generated code is held to a stricter bar than human code, requiring tests and disclosure, barring soundness-critical changes unless the author is a domain expert, and letting reviewers close non-compliant PRs. Disclosure of public LLM text is the enforceable bright line; authors self-declare LLM involvement, reviewers are not required to detect it, and harassment over LLM use is prohibited. The author frames the change as a response to reviewer bandwidth (1,281 open PRs), the loss of polished PRs as a signal of effort, and trust erosion from copy-paste round-tripping. He acknowledges he dislikes parts of the policy but argues written rules beat unwritten ones, and notes the leadership council may form a sub-team to manage future LLM policy.
novelty: Rust project formalizes explicit LLM contribution rules
audience: open-source maintainers and contributors grappling with AI-generated PRs

title: Humans missed 1 in 3 threats approving AI agent commands across 40k game runs
why: If you approve AI coding-agent commands under time pressure, this data says you will wave through roughly a third of real threats, and the exfiltration commands that actually leak credentials are the ones you miss most.
notes: Dataset: a browser game where the player is the human-in-the-loop, analyzed across 40,000 runs and 409,000 approve/deny decisions. Mean threat-catch accuracy was 66.3%; 32.9% of sessions ended net-negative; 7% of players approved every prompt.

Miss rate scaled inversely with obviousness: obvious destructive commands (rm -rf /, chmod -R 777 /) missed 11.7%, persistent mutation 23.8%, exfiltration/code execution 33.4%, scope violations (cat ~/.aws/credentials) 35.0%.

The most-missed threat was 'npm run analyze' at 64.7%, whose package.json script piped bundle output to curl POST https://api.bundle.track/report; the malicious payload was visible in the agent history log yet approved anyway. Pooled across three npm-script traps the miss rate was 52.5% (n=9,482) versus 28.4% for other exfil-style attacks, roughly doubling success.

Benign commands were routinely blocked, generating fatigue-inducing noise: npm config set registry blocked 59%, rm -rf dist/ 45%, kill $(lsof -t -i:3000) 43%. cat ~/.zshrc split players (approved 45.9%) because its risk depends on whether the user stores secrets there, which the agent cannot see.

Author's caveat: this is a time-boxed game where ~34% of commands were threats and players knew they were being tested, unlike real workflows where threats are rare, so numbers are comparative signal, not a field measurement. Cites Anthropic's own note that permission fatigue lowers per-approval attention over time.

Structural argument (attributed to HN commenter dns_snek): approving individual commands is weak because npm run/build executes arbitrary shell from package.json, and the agent can edit package.json, build.js, or node_modules unprompted; suggested mitigations are sandboxing and separating credentials from env/shell profiles.
summary: A developer built a browser game putting the player in the human-in-the-loop role for an AI coding agent, approving or denying commands under a clock, then analyzed 40,000 runs and 409,000 decisions. Players caught threats with a mean accuracy of 66.3%, missing about one in three; 32.9% of sessions ended net-negative and 7% approved everything. Miss rates tracked how obvious the danger looked: 11.7% for blatantly destructive commands versus 33-35% for exfiltration and credential-scope violations. The single most-missed threat was 'npm run analyze' (64.7%), which hid a curl exfiltration payload inside a package.json script; the payload was shown in the agent's history log but approved anyway, and such script-name disguises roughly doubled attack success. The piece argues per-command approval is a weak safeguard because familiar commands run arbitrary code the agent could have already tampered with, and because frequent blocking of benign commands (npm config set registry blocked 59%, rm -rf dist/ 45%) breeds the permission fatigue Anthropic itself has flagged. Caveats: it is a game with an artificially high ~34% threat rate and warned, time-pressured players, so the numbers are comparative rather than a real-world measurement.
novelty: quantified data showing human approval of AI agent commands fails ~1/3 of time
audience: engineers building or deploying human-in-the-loop AI agent permission systems

title: NVIDIA’s Vera Whitepaper Has a Thread Loose
why: If you plan capacity around Nvidia's Vera, the real x86 gap is roughly 1.9x memory bandwidth and a 3% two-socket integer-rate lead, not the 3x and 1.8x figures the whitepaper leads with.
notes: Olympus is a 10-wide Arm v9.2 out-of-order core: neural branch predictor, value prediction, memory renaming, six 128-bit SVE pipes, 96KB L1D, 2MB private L2 (~10-cycle), 88 cores on a monolithic die behind a 3.4TB/s fabric and 164MB system-level cache; memory is 8 SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X modules, up to 1.5TB and a claimed 1.2TB/s at ~50W.

Phoronix's May run (pre-production, one-day window, NVIDIA-chosen workloads, no power or frequency monitoring) put Vera's geomean 10% over a 5GHz EPYC 9575F, 1.55x a Xeon 6980P, and 1.63x Grace, the fastest public Arm server result so far.

Author faults the marketing, not the silicon: the SMT diagram wrongly paints traditional SMT as time-slicing that leaves resources idle; the '32 NUMA nodes' figure is AMD's optional max-granularity mode, not a default; value prediction, graph prefetching (Intel Data-Dependent Prefetcher since 2022) and neural branch prediction (AMD perceptrons since 2012) are prior art.

Benchmark reframing: four SPEC CPU 2026 components (CPython, GCC, LLVM, Cppcheck) are relabeled 'agentic benchmarks'; the 1.7-1.8x bars are per-physical-core (176 Vera cores vs 256 EPYC), while full estimated SPECrate 2026 Integer Base is 925 vs 898 for two EPYC 9755 sockets, a 3.0% system lead. Figure 24's '1.8x RL training' is an unlabeled row of tiles with no model, framework, or error bars.

Memory claim reworked: NVIDIA shows Turin topping out near 400 GB/s, but Chips and Cheese measured ~570 GB/s (93% of AMD's 614 GB/s theoretical), cutting Vera's lead from ~3x to ~1.9x total and from 4.1x to ~2.8x per core; against the 9575F head-node SKU per-core bandwidth is only ~40% better. Both chips hit ~92-93% of theoretical, so the advantage is memory interfaces, not the monolithic die.

Timing caveat: NVIDIA published July 21, AMD launched 6th Gen EPYC two days later; the 96-core EPYC 9686F offers 16 channels at DDR5-8000 or MRDIMM-12800 (1,024 or 1,638 GB/s/socket), exceeding Vera's bandwidth on some SKUs. Also noted: an Olympus core takes ~10,000 cycles to revert to single-thread mode after a sibling thread finishes.
summary: Chips and Cheese dissects NVIDIA's 45-page whitepaper for Vera, its first server CPU built on the in-house Olympus core (10-wide Arm v9.2, 88 cores monolithic, value prediction, graph prefetcher, 164MB shared cache, 8 LPDDR5X modules at a claimed 1.2TB/s and ~50W). The author's thesis: the hardware is genuinely fast, but the competitive argument is overstated. Specific rebuttals include a misleading SMT-as-time-slicing diagram, presenting AMD's optional 32-NUMA-node mode as an x86 default, relabeling four SPEC CPU 2026 integer tests as 'agentic benchmarks,' and citing undefined cross-ISA IPC counter ratios. title: OpenAI's super PAC is funding AI-generated news site attacking industry critics
why: A functioning AI-run "news wire" with fake reporter agents and self-scoring editorial software is already publishing political advocacy at scale, and its own leaked API shows the human review takes seconds, not judgment.
notes: Acutus (AcutusWire.com) launched Dec 29, 2025, and published 94 full-length articles in under four months with no masthead, bylines, or named editors; Pangram flagged 69% as fully AI-generated, 28% as partially, and only 3 as human-authored (Pangram's near-zero false-positive claim is self-reported by the vendor).

The site's React app exposes its editorial backend in client-side JS: fields like 'AI Background Context' and 'Question Prompts,' a 'Generate Story Draft' button, an AI quote-extractor, and a multi-pass AI review scored on AP style, quote accuracy, source verification, and 'acutus,' plus a fact-checking status.

The public endpoint acutuswire.com/api/wire leaks the full story database and per-article review logs; median time from first flagged issue to last resolution is 44 seconds and 10 seconds to publish; 42 of 94 stories were published despite the AI reviewer's own status reading 'needs_revision.'

The fake reporter 'Michael Chen' (reporter@acutuswire.com) is the site's 'AI interviewer'/'reporter agent'; it emailed Encode's Nathan Calvin offering only a 'written Q&A,' and Harvard's Joseph Fuller says he unknowingly gave quotes to it.

Author Tyler Johnston links Acutus to Patrick Hynes' PR firm Novus Public Affairs, whose client list includes Targeted Victory, the GOP firm whose CEO co-founded the $125M Leading The Future super PAC funded by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and a16z and run by OpenAI operative Chris Lehane; Hynes appears as an undisclosed 'expert' source in one Acutus article.

Roughly 15% of articles cover AI, echoing Leading The Future talking points (attacking Anthropic, blaming journalists for violence against OpenAI); the attribution to OpenAI's PAC is the author's inference, and OpenAI's usage policies prohibit political campaigning with its products.
summary: Model Republic's Tyler Johnston reports that Acutus (AcutusWire.com), an anonymously run "news wire" launched Dec 29, 2025, appears to be an AI content operation: Pangram flagged 69% of its 94 articles as fully AI-generated and 28% as partial, and the site's client-side JavaScript and a public API endpoint (/api/wire) expose an AI-driven pipeline with 'Generate Story Draft' buttons and a self-scoring editorial review whose timestamps show human oversight measured in seconds. A fake "reporter," Michael Chen, is actually the site's AI interviewer agent that solicited comment from AI-safety advocates including Encode's Nathan Calvin, while other quotes appear scraped from prior web content or fed in as convenient anonymous sources. Johnston traces the operation to Patrick Hynes' PR firm Novus Public Affairs, whose clients include Targeted Victory, the firm central to OpenAI's $125M Leading The Future super PAC, and notes AI-focused pieces mirror the PAC's anti-regulation talking points. He argues this would contradict OpenAI's own usage policies barring political campaigning, though the OpenAI connection is presented as inference from shared vendors, client overlaps, and technical fingerprints rather than direct proof. More than a third of the site's output, he writes, reads as paid advocacy aligned with a PR client list rather than journalism.

title: Why we write our own C and C++ inference engines
why: A 66 MiB C++ binary matches vLLM's throughput token-for-token and runs on 3 GiB less host memory, so the standard multi-gigabyte Python inference deploy is not the price of admission for competitive serving.
notes: vllm.cpp is a C++20 port of vLLM's V1 architecture (paged KV cache, continuous batching, prefix caching, scheduler, sampler) with no Python, PyTorch, or ggml at inference; self-reported benchmark on an NVIDIA GB10 running Qwen3.6-27B in NVFP4 (greedy, closed loop, vs vLLM in graphed not enforce-eager config) shows ties within a 0.5% noise band at concurrency 2-32, a 4.5% single-stream win, byte-identical output, and 24.88 vs 28.18 GiB peak host memory. Install footprint: 66 MiB binary vs 9.1 GiB virtualenv.

depth-anything.cpp (port of ByteDance Depth Anything 3) runs 1.31x faster than PyTorch on CPU (319.4 vs 416.9 ms infer), 363 vs 1328 MB RAM, 40 vs 749 ms load, on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D. The win came from caching two positional embeddings recomputed each forward via single-threaded scalar sin/cos/bicubic loops (~95 ms saved), not from faster kernels; on GPU it ties tuned cuDNN at 47.3 ms and only wins cold start.

Parity is treated as the ship gate before speed: 37 ctest parity cases correlate 1.0 with the reference, parakeet.cpp gates on WER 0 vs NeMo, and biometric ports match to cosine 1.000000 because a fourth-decimal embedding drift shifts threshold decisions and would force recomputing every enrolled template.

face-detect.cpp (SCRFD + ArcFace insightface buffalo chain in one GGUF) matches boxes/landmarks to 1 pixel and embeddings to cosine 1.000000 but runs 0.61-0.84x of onnxruntime on CPU; routing convolutions through cuDNN on GPU takes SCRFD from 14.8 to 6.4 ms for torch-cuDNN parity. voice-detect.cpp peaks at ~62 MB vs ~334 MB for the Python/torch/onnxruntime WeSpeaker path (~5.4x lower).

Stated cost: each of the 18 from-scratch engines is a separate repo with its own CI, benchmark suite, GGUF converter, and parity baselines, plus converter churn on new upstream checkpoints; ggml's generic CUDA conv/attention kernels trail cuDNN, so conv-heavy models need explicit cuDNN paths (parakeet.cpp GPU margin is median 1.25x vs a wider CPU margin).

Deployment is one shared library plus a GGUF file loaded via dlopen through purego with a flat C ABI, so there is no subprocess, gRPC hop, or interpreter in the serving path; llama.cpp, vLLM, whisper.cpp, MLX, and diffusers stay wrapped, with ports reserved for missing C++ implementations or when Python deps outweigh the model.
summary: LocalAI describes why 18 of its inference backends are from-scratch C/C++ ports rather than wrappers, and reports benchmarks for several. Its C++20 vllm.cpp reimplements vLLM's V1 serving stack (paged KV cache, continuous batching, prefix caching) in a 66 MiB binary versus a 9.1 GiB virtualenv, and on an NVIDIA GB10 running Qwen3.6-27B in NVFP4 it ties vLLM throughput within a 0.5% noise band with token-identical output and lower peak memory (24.88 vs 28.18 GiB). depth-anything.cpp beats PyTorch by 1.31x on CPU at 27% of the memory, a win attributed to caching positional embeddings the reference recomputed each forward, not to better kernels; the article notes GPU GEMMs are a wash and ggml's generic CUDA conv/attention kernels trail cuDNN. Biometric ports face-detect.cpp and voice-detect.cpp match reference embeddings to cosine 1.000000 (voice-detect at ~5.4x lower memory) even though face-detect runs 0.61-0.84x of onnxruntime on CPU, because exact parity makes them drop-in replacements. The stated method is fixed: convert weights to one GGUF, port the graph with per-component parity gates, profile and optimize only after parity holds, and expose a flat C ABI loaded via dlopen. All figures are self-reported vendor benchmarks with methodology described but not independently verified.
novelty: rigorous benchmarks showing C++ ports match/beat Python inference stacks
audience: ML infra engineers deciding between Python and native inference stacks

title: Show HN: Nightcrawler – A local AI pentesting agent running on a smartphone
why: A full pentest drop box now fits in a rooted OnePlus 8 running a 1.2B model on the phone's GPU with no cloud, so autonomous, offline network attacks no longer need a laptop or an API key.
notes: Inference is 100% local: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Heretic (Q8_0) runs on the Adreno 650 GPU via OpenCL at a self-reported 115 tok/s prompt, 13 tok/s generation; Android throttles the GPU ~6x on battery, so a GPU governor daemon forces max clocks and auto-throttles at 15% battery.

The agent loop asks the model for one REASONING/COMMAND per turn, then a two-layer scope proxy validates each command against IP/port/host scope and a destructive-command blocklist before a Kali MCP server runs tools like nmap, curl, smbclient.

Ships a 24,956-entry CVE database for version-aware matching and 27 multi-step playbooks; playbooks execute directly, bypassing the LLM, to compensate for the 1.2B model's stated ~50% command-success rate (garbage/duplicate/stuck detection triggers context resets).

Stealth-first design: nmap -T2 only, weighted host rotation, cover traffic, passive mDNS/NBNS/DHCP/ARP capture, and a dashboard that spoofs nginx headers and returns empty 404s to connections from the target network.

Optional offline WiFi-breach mode cracks WPA2 with an external USB adapter (Ralink RT3572, Pwnagotchi-inspired); requires rooted Android via Magisk, Kali NetHunter, 12GB+ RAM, and a custom MAC80211 monitor-mode kernel.

Self-reported results from 72+ hours across multiple networks: 30+ hosts discovered per network, 2,000+ commands executed, 10+ vulnerabilities found, memory stable at 35-50MB; numbers are the author's, with no external methodology or third-party validation.
summary: Nightcrawler is an open-source (MIT) autonomous penetration-testing agent that runs entirely on a rooted Android phone (tested on a OnePlus 8, Snapdragon 865) under Kali NetHunter, with no cloud connectivity. A 1.2B-parameter local model (LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Heretic) running on the Adreno 650 GPU via OpenCL drives an agent loop that picks targets, issues one shell command per turn through a Kali MCP server, and parses output into a SQLite host memory; a scope proxy plus destructive-command filter enforce authorization boundaries. It bundles a 24,956-entry CVE database, 27 direct-execution exploit playbooks, stealth measures (nmap -T2, host rotation, cover traffic, passive broadcast capture), a Flask C2 dashboard, and an optional Pwnagotchi-style WPA2-cracking mode via a USB WiFi adapter. The author reports ~50% LLM command-success (mitigated by garbage/stuck detection and playbook fallbacks) and on-device speeds of 115 tok/s prompt and 13 tok/s generation, with a GPU governor daemon to counter Android's ~6x battery throttling. Self-reported runs over 72+ hours claim 30+ hosts and 10+ vulnerabilities per network with stable 35-50MB memory. The project stresses it is for authorized testing only and provides a dry-run mock mode; all performance and results figures are the author's and lack third-party verification.
novelty: fully autonomous local-LLM pentest agent running entirely offline on a phone
audience: security researchers and red-teamers interested in edge/local AI agents

title: What Happened to HackerOne?
why: If you submit to a bug bounty platform, this insider account argues your reports now feed an automated triage system whose behavior changes based on past outcomes, despite HackerOne's repeated claims that it does not train AI on researcher data.
notes: Author is a bug bounty hunter since 2017 who ran multiple large HackerOne programs from 2018 to 2025, writing from both the researcher and program-manager sides; all claims are first-hand and self-reported, not independently documented.

Business timeline per the piece: founded 2011 by Jobert Abma and Michiel Prins; Live Hacking Events ran 2017-2020; ~$160M raised via seed rounds roughly every two years from 2014 to 2022; monetization pivot around 2020-2021 shifted from a 20% bounty cut to capacity-based fees and multi-year contracts with claimed 30-60% renewal discounts.

The author frames Hai as an OpenAI wrapper and says HackerOne rebranded around a self-coined category, 'CTEM' (Continuous Threat Exposure Management), while co-founders Abma and Prins were sidelined despite executive titles.

The core contradiction: after a February 2026 ToS change (flagged by hacker zseano) let reports train AI models, CTO/co-founder Alex Rice and CEO Kara Sprague (ex-F5 CPO, replaced Marten Mickos late 2024) publicly denied any training/fine-tuning on researcher data; the author quotes a HackerOne PM saying all reports run through an AI intake agent that stores rejection reasons and 'learns from behaviour' to adjust future recommendations.

A June 2026 'HackerOne Continuous Testing' page reportedly claimed agents are 'sharpened using context from HackerOne's 12+ years of real-world vulnerability data and your prior H1 Bounty findings,' language the company later edited and reframed as scope/recon mapping, not vulnerability discovery from researcher submissions.
summary: A longtime HackerOne researcher and program manager argues the platform declined from a hacker-first community into a sales-driven B2B company after VC pressure (~$160M raised 2014-2022) forced a monetization pivot around 2020-2021, ending its 2017-2020 Live Hacking Events, burning out top triagers, and stagnating platform development. The author says leadership sidelined co-founders Jobert Abma and Michiel Prins, replaced CEO Marten Mickos with ex-F5 CPO Kara Sprague in late 2024, built an OpenAI-wrapper assistant called Hai, and rebranded around a self-coined 'CTEM' category. The central dispute concerns a February 2026 ToS change that appeared to allow training AI on report data: executives including CTO Alex Rice and CEO Sprague publicly denied training or fine-tuning on researcher submissions. The author counters with quotes from a HackerOne product manager describing an AI intake agent that processes all reports and stores rejection reasons to influence future recommendations, and a since-edited June 2026 product page citing '12+ years of real-world vulnerability data' and prior findings. The piece contends HackerOne's denials rely on a narrow definition of 'training' that is functionally equivalent to learning from researcher data. All assertions are the author's personal account and quoted chat/blog statements, not independently verified.
novelty: insider account of HackerOne's decline from community-first to profit-driven

title: AI helped produce two proofs for the same cryptography problem
why: Two research groups pointing the same model at the same open problem produced near-identical proofs 3 hours 18 minutes apart, a concrete preview of AI collapsing the timeline and independence of theoretical discovery.
notes: Both preprints credit OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra with the core proof ideas and construction; OpenAI says the Ultra system coordinates four AI agents in parallel by default. Both papers are unreviewed and self-report that the humans verified and take responsibility for the claims.

The result is in unclonable encryption, a quantum-crypto subfield built on Broadbent and Lord's 2019 framework: the papers claim an efficient scheme with the sought stronger security and without prior caveats. Earlier work showed unclonable encryption was possible but was inefficient or needed extra assumptions.

Different workflows, same model: MIT's Seyoon Ragavan ran hands-on two-hour sessions, checking and redirecting the model; UCSB's Ananth and UCLA's Sahai used a bespoke UCLA system for AI-driven propose-and-critique cycles. The open question was posed weeks earlier at Berkeley's Simons Institute.

Credit and novelty caveat: the model's first proposed construction turned out to duplicate a scheme Broadbent's group had already published earlier in 2026; the new contribution was proving the stronger security, not inventing the scheme.
The two teams learned of the overlap before either paper was public, via UCSB student Yao-Ting Lin, and are discussing merging into a single conference submission.
Researchers voice concern about 'haves and have-nots': the automatable work is what Broadbent would normally assign to graduate students, and Ananth says he worries for 'the current crop.'
summary: On the same day, two teams submitted arXiv preprints solving the same open problem in unclonable encryption, an efficient scheme with stronger security and no extra assumptions, and both credited OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra for the core ideas. MIT's Seyoon Ragavan worked iteratively in two-hour human-checked sessions, while UCSB's Prabhanjan Ananth and UCLA's Amit Sahai used a bespoke UCLA propose-and-critique system; the papers landed 3 hours 18 minutes apart. Both problems traced to an open question posed weeks earlier at Berkeley's Simons Institute, and neither paper has been peer-reviewed. The work builds on Broadbent and Lord's 2019 framework, but the model's first proposed construction duplicated a scheme Broadbent's group had already published in 2026, so the claimed contribution is the stronger-security proof rather than the construction itself. Researchers found the results convincing but raised concerns about credit, independent discovery, and the erosion of work traditionally assigned to graduate students. The two teams are discussing merging their papers for a conference.
novelty: two independent teams get near-identical AI-generated proofs within hours

title: Spectral Compute Aims to Set CUDA Free. Will It Succeed?
why: A drop-in NVCC replacement that recompiles CUDA to AMD (and other) accelerators without a source rewrite would let HPC and ML shops keep existing CUDA code while shopping for cheaper hardware, and the vendor claims ~6x over AMD's own HIPIFY path.
notes: SCALE, from London-based Spectral Compute (founded 2018, ~30 employees, $6M raised), is a Clang/LLVM-based drop-in replacement for Nvidia's NVCC that recompiles CUDA rather than translating source; it verifies output numerically against NVCC to judge correctness.
Company-published benchmarks claim nearly 6x performance over converting CUDA to AMD's ROCm via HIPIFY; no methodology is described in the article, so treat as a vendor self-report.

Positioning against rivals (per Spectral): HIPIFY ignores PTX, Nvidia's assembly layer for deep hardware support; Intel-origin SYCLomatic migrates ~90% of code, leaving 10% manual; ZLUDA works on compiled binaries as middleware, hurting performance and facing legal questions.

Coverage so far is AMD GPUs plus Nvidia (Spectral argues Nvidia leaves software optimization on the table to sell hardware); unnamed third-party AI accelerators are in progress, and PyTorch support was expected later in the month.

SCALE has run on Oak Ridge's Frontier exascale system; the core CUDA product is supported but specialized libraries (cuDNN, cuTENSOR, cuDF) are still being added. Commercial customers pay; academic and non-profit users get the toolkit free.
Spectral joined the Nvidia Inception program in June 2026 and describes itself as 'truly neutral'; SCALE has shipped for only about two years, so there is no long track record.
summary: Spectral Compute, a London startup founded in 2018 with about 30 employees and $6M raised, makes SCALE, a Clang/LLVM-based drop-in replacement for Nvidia's NVCC compiler that recompiles CUDA code to run on non-Nvidia hardware, currently AMD GPUs with unnamed AI accelerators in progress. The company frames its approach as a clean-room reimplementation applying standard CPU compiler techniques to GPUs, and it verifies recompiled output numerically against NVCC. Its published benchmarks claim nearly 6x performance over AMD's HIPIFY-to-ROCm conversion path, though no methodology is given. Spectral contrasts SCALE with HIPIFY (ignores PTX), SYCLomatic (~90% automated migration), and ZLUDA (binary-level middleware with performance and legal issues). SCALE has run on Oak Ridge's Frontier, supports core CUDA with specialized libraries like cuDNN and cuDF still being added, and PyTorch support was expected later in the month. Spectral joined Nvidia's Inception program in June 2026 and sells to commercial users while giving the toolkit to academic and non-profit users; the product has shipped only about two years, so its track record is short.
